1.text:
What Tries to Kill Astronauts?

In Deck 24, you figured out how far and how long a trip to the stars would take. But getting there is only half the problem. You also have to survive the trip.

This deck covers the hazards of space travel. Our driving question: what tries to kill astronauts, and how do we fight back? We'll look at radiation, what weightlessness does to your body, flying grit and junk, and the lessons NASA learned the hard way.

2.text:
Helmet Off in Space?

Imagine this: you remove your helmet in space. What gets you first?

Vote A to D: A) freezing, B) boiling blood, C) radiation, or D) no air. Movies have shown every dramatic answer you can think of. Lock in your vote and keep it in mind as you read.

3.text:
Today I Can...

This is your checklist. Copy these as "I can" statements and rate yourself at the end.

I can name the radiation risks of a Mars trip. I can explain how fields, air and rock shield us. I can describe what weightlessness does to a body. And I can explain how one crash can start a debris chain.

4.text:
Part 1: Radiation

Radiation is an invisible danger. You can't see it, feel it or smell it, but it adds up over time. In Deck 14 you learned about flares and space weather from the Sun.

Our question for this part: what stops radiation on Earth, and what stops it out there?

5.text:
Radiation Adds Up

On the surface of Mars, you'd get about 100× Earth's radiation. A whole Mars mission adds up to about 1 Sv (sievert, a unit of radiation dose).

Compare the numbers in mSv (millisieverts, thousandths of a sievert). 1 year on Earth gives about 2.4 mSv. A 6-month trip to Mars gives about 330 mSv each way, so about 660 mSv there and back. 500 days on Mars gives about 320 mSv. The whole mission, there and back, is about 1 Sv.

For scale, the limit for radiation workers on Earth is 20 mSv/yr. That's why radiation is called the greatest danger to humans heading to Mars.

6.text:
What Shields Us

On Earth, a magnetic field plus air protect us. The magnetic field, made in Earth's iron core, steers charged particles away, and the thick air absorbs much of the rest.

What about a spacesuit? Spacesuits stop heat and grit, not radiation. Blocking radiation would take a dense, heavy layer.

Did you know? Most cosmic rays, the fast particles zipping through space, are thought to be sped up by supernova blasts.

7.text:
Live Underground

If suits can't stop radiation, what can? Rock. A lava tube is a natural tunnel left when flowing lava drained away.

Rock blocks the radiation. Lava tubes on the Moon and Mars could become ready-made shelters, letting astronauts live underground with tons of rock overhead.

8.text:
Check for Understanding: Part 1

Think about what a spacesuit can and can't do. Why can't a thicker spacesuit fix the radiation problem?

Is it A) it would be too heavy to move in, B) radiation passes around it, C) suits already block it, or D) radiation is harmless in space? Use Slides 6 and 7 to decide.

9.text:
Part 2: The Body Without Weight

Astronauts float because they're falling around Earth, as you learned earlier in the course. That sounds fun, but your body was built for gravity.

Our question for this part: what happens to bones and blood when nothing feels heavy?

10.text:
Weightless Bodies Weaken

Compare a body on Earth to a body after months in orbit. Without weight to work against, muscles shrink and bones thin.

Fluids float upward, toward the head. That changes the eyes, the heart and balance. It's like your body is always standing on its head.

That's why astronauts on the space station exercise about two hours a day.

11.text:
Spin to Make Gravity

So how could we fix weightlessness on a long trip? Spin a ring-shaped ship: the floor presses up like gravity.

It's the same feeling you get on a spinning carnival ride that pins you against the wall. In a ring-shaped ship, called a torus, the outer wall becomes the floor.

12.text:
Hopping, Not Walking

What about walking on the Moon or Mars, where gravity is weak but not zero? Compared with Earth, low gravity turns every step into a bouncy hop, especially on the Moon.

Any small push-off sends you upward, so astronauts hop and skip instead of walking normally.

Did you know? Apollo astronauts found that a bunny hop was often the easiest way to get around on the Moon.

13.text:
Part 3: Grit and Junk

Space isn't empty. It's full of tiny rocks and, near Earth, our own trash.

Our question for this part: how can a grain of dust punch through a spaceship?

14.text:
Tiny but Deadly

The recipe is simple: tiny grain + huge speed = hole in the hull.

Micrometeoroids are tiny, but they move incredibly fast, often tens of kilometers per second. At that speed, a speck of grit can hit with the punch of a bullet and puncture a hull or a suit.

Now think back to your hook vote on Slide 2. What would really happen first without a helmet?

15.text:
The Kessler Chain Reaction

It goes in three steps. 1, Crash: one collision. 2, Debris: a cloud of fragments. 3, More crashes: each one makes more debris.

Each crash sets up the next, like a line of dominoes. This is called the Kessler Syndrome, and it threatens low orbits first.

That puts weather, imaging and internet satellites at risk, the ones we depend on every day.

16.text:
Door Blows Open: Instant Fog

What happens if a spaceship door suddenly blows open? Pressure drops, air expands and cools, and water vapor condenses: a cloud.

It's the same physics that makes clouds on Earth. Rising air expands and cools, and its moisture condenses. In a spaceship, it all happens in an instant.

17.text:
Part 4: Remembering the Crews

This part is in memory of the 17 astronauts lost in NASA spacecraft accidents on Apollo 1, Challenger and Columbia.

Each loss taught hard lessons. Our question: what did we learn, and how did spaceflight change?

18.text:
In Memory

Before any causes or lessons, we pause to remember them by name.

Apollo 1 (1967): Gus Grissom, Ed White and Roger Chaffee.

Challenger (1986): Dick Scobee, Michael Smith, Judith Resnik, Ellison Onizuka, Ronald McNair, Gregory Jarvis and Christa McAuliffe.

Columbia (2003): Rick Husband, William McCool, Michael Anderson, Kalpana Chawla, David Brown, Laurel Clark and Ilan Ramon.

19.text:
What Each Mission Taught Us

Each accident had a specific engineering cause, and fixing it made spaceflight safer. The green tags show what changed after each mission.

1967, Apollo 1: an oxygen fire during a test. Afterward came a new air mix and a quick-opening hatch. 1970, Apollo 13: an oxygen tank exploded, but the crew made it home safe. The oxygen tank was redesigned.

1986, Challenger: cold seals failed in a rocket booster. NASA added new joints and launch rules. 2003, Columbia: a damaged wing broke apart on the way home. Now crews do wing checks in orbit.

20.text:
Speak Up

On launch day for Challenger, it was 36 °F. Engineers had said: no launch below 53 °F. Their warning was overruled.

The cold stiffened the rubber seals, and the result was a disaster. The lesson goes far beyond rockets: good data only helps if the people making decisions listen. If you see a problem, speak up.

21.text:
Student Task: Design a Mars Base

Now put it all together. Design a Mars base that protects its crew, using evidence from this deck.

Plan four parts: A, pick a site. B, shield from radiation. C, keep bodies strong. D, avoid debris and leaks. For example, where could rock help? How could exercise or spinning help?

22.text:
Exit Ticket

Show what you learned about surviving space.

First, name one hazard a Mars crew faces and one way to protect them. Second, pick one mission from Part 4. What was the cause, and what changed afterward?

Then look back at your "I can" list from Slide 3 and rate yourself 1 to 3 on each one.

23.text:
The Standards Behind This Lesson

This lesson follows the Indiana Earth and Space Science standards. Here's what they ask, in plain words.

ES.1.1: explain how we study space by observing every kind of light with different telescopes and tools. ES.2.2: describe the objects in the solar system, like planets, moons, comets, asteroids and protoplanets, and how the solar system is organized. Know that planets orbit other stars, and some drift with no star at all.
